The Story of the Prideful Wife

I bow to Lord Jina, who bears pure omniscient knowledge, and I write the story of one who suffered bad results from pride. Those who hear this story and strive to abandon pride will gain happiness.

King Vrushabhdhvaj of Banaras cared for the welfare of his subjects and was very wise. His queen was Vasumati, who was very beautiful. The king loved her deeply.

On the banks of the Ganga, there was a village named Palas. In it lived a cowherd named Ashok. This cowherd used to give the king about a thousand pots full of ghee as village tax. His wife Nanda was not loved by him, because she was barren. And truly, however beautiful or virtuous a wife may be, without children she lacks splendour, nor does her husband's full love rest upon her. She is considered fruitless, like a vine without fruit.

Seeing his first wife childless, Ashok the cowherd married again. His new wife's name was Sunanda. For some time, the two co-wives got along out of worldly propriety, but when quarrelling became constant, Ashok, tired of them, divided all his property equally between them. Nanda had to live in a separate house, while Sunanda stayed with Ashok.

Nanda had one great quality — she was sensible and kept her milking vessels very clean. She loved cleanliness. Besides this, she treated her servant cowherds with great love, considering them not as servants but as family. She honoured them greatly and kept them happy with gifts on every festival. Therefore, the cowherds loved her too and did her work as if it were their own. When the year ended, Nanda would give her half — five hundred pots of ghee — to her master as her annual tax.

But Sunanda lacked all these qualities. She was very proud of her beauty. Besides this, she was very fond of luxury. All her time was spent in adornment and decoration. She did not like to do any work with her own hands. Everything was done by servants. Even then, her behaviour toward her servants was not good. She always scolded them, insulted some, and abused others.

When the year came to measure the ghee, Sunanda's pots were found to be fewer than the required number. Her servants, unhappy with her treatment, had not put their full effort into her work. Meanwhile, Nanda's five hundred pots were perfectly measured, clean, and full. The king, hearing of this, honoured Nanda greatly and punished Sunanda for her negligence and pride.

Sunanda's pride in her beauty and her neglect of duty led to her downfall. She lost her husband's respect and the loyalty of her servants. Nanda, through her humility, cleanliness, and kind treatment of others, gained prosperity and honour.

This story teaches that pride — especially pride in beauty — is a great obstacle to success. Sunanda's reliance on her looks and her neglect of her duties led to her ruin. Meanwhile, Nanda, though not beautiful and initially disadvantaged, through her good qualities and proper conduct, gained prosperity. The wise should cultivate humility, cleanliness, and kindness, for these are the true sources of success.
